transcript.heading: News Report One (British Female)
paras: A major telecommunications company has announced plans to provide free high-speed internet access to one million low-income households across the country by the end of next year. The initiative, called "Connect for All," will offer internet speeds of at least 100 megabits per second to eligible families with school-aged children or adults enrolled in job training programs. Company officials say the program is designed to close the digital divide that became particularly apparent during the pandemic, when millions of students struggled to attend online classes without reliable internet. The company is investing 2 billion dollars in the program, including infrastructure upgrades in underserved rural and urban areas, and will also provide low-cost computers and digital literacy training to participating households. Education advocates have praised the announcement, noting that internet access is increasingly essential for completing homework, applying for jobs, and accessing government services. Several other telecommunications providers have indicated they are considering similar programs following this announcement.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (American Male)
paras: Firefighters in California made significant progress this weekend containing a massive wildfire that has burned over 50,000 acres of forest land in the northern part of the state. The fire, which started a week ago during a period of extremely hot, dry weather and strong winds, destroyed at least 80 homes and forced thousands of residents to evacuate. At the peak of the blaze, more than 3,000 firefighters were deployed, supported by aircraft dropping water and fire retardant. Fire officials reported this morning that they have now established containment lines around 65 percent of the fire, up from just 20 percent on Friday. Cooler temperatures and calmer winds over the weekend helped crews gain the upper hand. Mandatory evacuation orders are being gradually lifted as firefighters secure affected areas, though residents are being warned to watch for falling trees and other hazards as they return home. Fire investigators are still working to determine the exact cause of the blaze, though they have said it does not appear to be suspicious.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Female)
paras: The International Olympic Committee announced this morning that Brisbane, Australia, has been selected as the host city for the 2032 Summer Olympic Games. Brisbane was chosen over competing bids from several other cities following a vote by IOC members in Tokyo. The Australian city already has approximately 80 percent of the required venues in place, including existing stadiums, aquatic centers, and sports facilities, which significantly reduced the projected cost of hosting the games. Organizers estimate the event will generate over 10 billion dollars for the local economy and create tens of thousands of jobs in construction, tourism, and hospitality. Brisbane becomes the third Australian city to host the Summer Olympics, following Melbourne in 1956 and Sydney in 2000. Queensland state officials have already announced plans for infrastructure improvements, including upgrades to public transportation and new athletes' village facilities, designed to leave lasting benefits for local communities after the games conclude. Preparations are expected to begin immediately, with organizers emphasizing a commitment to sustainability and fiscal responsibility.

paras: Woman (Waitress): Good evening! Welcome to The Blue Olive. Do you have a reservation, or would you like a table for two?
Man (Customer): Hi there. We have a reservation under the name Peterson, for 7 o'clock. There should be two of us, but we might be joined by another friend later if that's okay.

Woman: Let me check... Yes, Peterson, party of two, table for four just in case. Right this way, please. Here are your menus. Would you like to start with something to drink? We have a selection of cocktails, wine, beer, and non-alcoholic beverages.
Man: I'll have a glass of your house red wine, please. What about you, Sarah?

Woman (Sarah): I'll just have sparkling water with lemon, thank you. I'm driving tonight. Oh, wait—could you tell me about the soup of the day? I see it listed on the board but didn't catch the description.

Woman (Waitress): Certainly. Today's soup is a roasted tomato and basil bisque, made with locally grown tomatoes. It's creamy and vegetarian. Our special tonight is grilled salmon with roasted vegetables and quinoa, which is very popular.

Woman (Waitress): The risotto does have a small amount of parmesan cheese, but no heavy cream. It should be fine for mild lactose intolerance. I can ask the chef to make it without cheese if you prefer, though.
Woman (Sarah): A little parmesan is fine. Thank you.

paras: Man (Ryan): Hey Megan, have you finished putting together your schedule for next semester yet? I'm trying to finalize mine before registration opens tomorrow.

Woman (Megan): I'm still working on it, actually. I have to take two required classes for my major—Advanced Statistics and Research Methods—but those are only offered at certain times, which is making it tricky to fit in electives. Did you manage to get everything you wanted?

Man: Sort of. I got into the Creative Writing workshop I was hoping for, which is on Tuesday and Thursday afternoons. But the Political Science seminar I wanted is already full, so I'm on the waitlist. I'm thinking of taking a philosophy class as a backup—Philosophy of Mind sounds really interesting, and it fulfills one of my general education requirements.

Woman: Oh, I took Philosophy of Mind last year with Professor Davies, and it was one of my favorite classes! It's pretty challenging—there's a lot of reading, and you have to write three long papers—but Professor Davies is an amazing lecturer, and the discussions are always fascinating. I definitely recommend it.
Man: That's good to hear. How heavy is the reading? I'm taking 15 credits next semester, so I don't want to be completely overwhelmed.

Woman: It's probably about 50 pages a week, but most of it is really interesting, so it doesn't feel like work. And the professor is really fair about grading—if you participate in discussions and show you've done the reading, you'll do fine. Have you registered for any online classes? I'm taking one online history class to give me more flexibility with my part-time job schedule.

Man: I was thinking about it, but I've heard mixed things about online classes. Some friends say they're easier, but others say it's harder to stay motivated without going to class in person. What's your experience been like?

Woman: I like them because you can do the work whenever fits your schedule, but you have to be really self-disciplined. It's easy to fall behind if you don't keep up with the weekly assignments. I'd recommend taking only one online class at a time at first to see how you like it.

transcript.heading: Passage One (British Male)
paras: Stargazing—observing the night sky with the naked eye or with binoculars and telescopes—is one of humanity's oldest pastimes, connecting us to the universe and to people throughout history who looked up at the same stars. Unfortunately, for millions of people living in cities and suburbs, light pollution has made it difficult or impossible to see more than a handful of the brightest stars. Artificial lighting from streetlights, buildings, billboards, and cars creates a diffuse glow in the sky that drowns out the light from faint stars, planets, and the Milky Way. Studies estimate that more than 80 percent of the world's population lives under light-polluted skies, and in many major cities, people can see fewer than a dozen stars on a clear night. However, there are still ways to enjoy stargazing even if you live in an urban area. First, try to find a local park or open area away from bright streetlights, preferably with a clear view of the horizon. Even a short drive to a less developed area can dramatically improve visibility. Second, give your eyes time to adapt to the dark—it typically takes about 20 to 30 minutes for your eyes to fully adjust and see fainter objects. Avoid looking at phone screens during this time, as blue light from devices will reset your dark adaptation. Binoculars are an excellent and relatively affordable tool for beginning stargazers, revealing craters on the moon, Jupiter's moons, and many deep-sky objects that are invisible to the naked eye. Many communities have local astronomy clubs that host public stargazing events, often with larger telescopes available for visitors to use. These clubs can also provide guidance on what to look for in each season.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (American Female)
paras: Walt Disney, the animator, entrepreneur, and cultural icon, was born in Chicago in 1901 and would go on to create one of the most recognizable entertainment companies in the world. Disney developed an early interest in drawing as a child, taking art classes as a teenager and working as a commercial illustrator after serving in World War I. In the 1920s, he moved to California and, with his brother Roy, founded the Disney Brothers Studio, which would later become The Walt Disney Company. Disney's first major success came with the creation of Mickey Mouse in 1928, a character who would become the studio's mascot and a global cultural symbol. Under Disney's leadership, the studio produced the first full-length synchronized sound cartoon, *Steamboat Willie*, and later the first full-color cartoon. In 1937, Disney released *Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs*, the first full-length animated feature film in English, which was a massive commercial and critical success despite industry skepticism that audiences would sit through a feature-length cartoon. Over the following decades, Disney studios produced classic films including *Fantasia*, *Bambi*, *Cinderella*, and *Mary Poppins*. Beyond film, Disney pursued his vision of a family amusement park, which led to the opening of Disneyland in California in 1955. Walt Disney World in Florida opened in 1971, five years after Disney's death from lung cancer in 1966. While Disney has been widely celebrated for his creative vision and contributions to entertainment and animation, his legacy has also been the subject of debate, with critics discussing aspects of his personal life and the company's labor practices. Nevertheless, Disney's work continues to shape popular culture and family entertainment worldwide.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Male)
paras: Urban farming—the practice of growing food and sometimes raising animals in and around cities—has grown rapidly in popularity over the past 15 years as people seek greater connection to their food, more sustainable food systems, and stronger local communities. Urban farms take many forms, from small container gardens on balconies and windowsills to larger community gardens in vacant lots, rooftop farms on top of buildings, and even commercial urban farms that sell produce to local restaurants and farmers' markets. The benefits of urban farming are numerous. Environmentally, growing food in cities reduces the transportation distance food travels from farm to plate, cutting carbon emissions from trucks and refrigeration. Urban gardens also help reduce the urban heat island effect by replacing concrete and asphalt with plants that provide shade and cool the air through evaporation. Green spaces created by urban farms can also manage stormwater, reducing flooding and filtering pollutants before they reach waterways. Socially, community gardens bring neighbors together across ages and backgrounds, creating shared public spaces where people can connect and build relationships. For neighborhoods lacking access to fresh, affordable produce—areas often called food deserts—urban farms can provide nutritious fruits and vegetables that would otherwise be unavailable. Many urban agriculture programs also provide job training and employment opportunities for local residents, particularly young people. Despite these benefits, urban farmers face challenges including limited access to land, potential soil contamination in former industrial areas, zoning restrictions, and limited access to water. However, many cities are now creating policies to support urban agriculture, including providing access to public land, offering tax incentives, and changing zoning laws to permit gardening and small-scale farming.
